Patient demographics:
  age: 32
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Nurse
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 75

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it

Vignette:
Komal, a 32-year-old South Asian woman and nurse, has been struggling with her mental health since she experienced a man-made disaster at work. The traumatic event occurred during her night shift when there was an explosion in the hospital’s chemical storage room, leading to toxic fumes that spread through the building, causing panic and chaos among staff and patients alike. Komal vividly recalls the moment she realized something was wrong: the acrid smell of burning chemicals filled the air as alarms blared. She remembers rushing into action without hesitation, trying to evacuate patients from her ward. However, the memory is so extreme that it feels surreal to her; it’s hard for Komal to believe this actually happened to her. The fragmented nature of her recollection makes it difficult for her to piece together what exactly transpired during those chaotic moments. For instance, she remembers leading a patient out of his room but cannot recall the sequence of events afterward. These disconnected pieces create an overwhelming sense of disorientation and disbelief when she tries to revisit that night. Since the incident, Komal has found herself pushing away memories before they can fully surface. She often catches herself blocking out parts of the story whenever someone asks about what happened. This habit has led her to avoid certain triggers in her environment, such as the smell of cleaning chemicals or loud sirens, both of which remind her too vividly of that night. In her daily work at the hospital, Komal’s fear and avoidance have had significant consequences. She finds herself increasingly hesitant about handling emergency situations, even those unrelated to chemical spills. Her colleagues have noticed a change in her demeanor; she is more withdrawn during patient care and has been avoiding assignments that require her to be on high alert. The trauma has also affected her personal life. Komal’s relationships with friends and family have become strained as she struggles to open up about what she experienced. She feels isolated, as if no one can truly understand the magnitude of her fear and confusion. Her avoidance extends beyond work; she avoids crowded places where she might feel trapped or overwhelmed. Komal had come to believe that she was not strong enough to cope with the aftermath of the disaster. The memory’s fragmented quality leaves her feeling like a part of herself is missing, as if she cannot fully integrate what happened into her identity. What frightened her most was the possibility of reliving such an intense experience again and being unable to handle it. Finally, the mounting pressure from work and the persistent intrusive memories pushed Komal to seek help. She is most hoping for a way to regain control over her thoughts and fears, to find peace in knowing that she can manage the haunting memories without them dictating her life. Through therapy, Komal aims to make sense of what happened, reconnect with those around her, and rediscover her strength as a nurse and an individual.
